Affected Vendors

Affected Products
Server
Vulnerability Details
This vulnerability allows local attackers to disclose sensitive information on affected installations of X.Org Server. An attacker must first obtain the ability to execute low-privileged code on the target system in order to exploit this vulnerability.
The specific flaw exists within the BufFileRawSkip function. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in a read past the end of an allocated data structure. An attacker can leverage this in conjunction with other vulnerabilities to execute arbitrary code in the context of root.

items.text: aff-wg published: Adding a little more… zip
items.title: Adding a little more… zip
items.content:
I’ve got another
Crystal Palace
and
Tradecraft Garden
update. Release number 17! This release adds .zip file encapsulation of projects and components, dispatch tables, and entry point AOP for PIC and PICOs.
.zip Pathing
One of the goals of Crystal Palace is to demonstrate a standard unit of tradecraft that can mix and match with capability and other tradecraft. This release moves us a little closer to this goal with .zip pathing support.
Crystal Palace now has the ability to pull resources and call .specs contained within .zip files. In paths, file.zip! becomes a folder when ! is present.
/path/to/foo.zip!/project/build.spec
This path refers to project/build.spec within foo.zip. This convention works throughout Crystal Palace. The only restriction is you can’t reference .zip paths within a .zip path. You get one .zip traversal per path.
To go with this, Crystal Palace now accepts .zip files anywhere you’d otherwise use a .spec. A .zip file by itself will run main.spec by default.
If you like the convenience of main.spec, but don’t want to rework your project’s folder structure to put a .spec at the top-level, I have you covered. Populate main.spec with:
delegate "path/to/build.spec"
delegate is a top-level command (it lives outside of a label) and it’s expected to exist by itself. The delegate command parses and runs the specified file in place of the current one. The new linker context inherits everything about the specified file (e.g., path, meta-info, labels, etc.).
The end result of this is that .zip files are first-class citizens in Crystal Palace. And, you now have freedom to package components and modules into self-contained .zips that are capable of working with and referencing each other.
Dispatch Tables
Dispatch Tables are a tool to dynamically register modules in Crystal Palace.
dispatch associates a function with a table and a linker-tracked integer ID:
dispatch
"main"
0x01
"foo"
dispatch
"main"
0x02
"bar"
dispatch
"main"
0x03
"baz"
The __dispatch_main intrinsic expands inline to resolve an ID to a local function pointer:
FARPROC __dispatch_main(DWORD id);
Dispatch tables are scoped to the current object on the stack. They’re not global. You can create as many tables as you like.
Thanks Daniel for
suggesting this
.
Entry Point Redirects
Crystal Palace’s redirect is a tool to rewrite calls and references to function A to instead call or reference function B. Like attach, redirect supports chaining too.
This release expands redirect’s scope and the logic now applies to a PIC and PICO entry point (e.g., go) and PICO exported functions.
LSH
catch handlers are targetable with redirect too.
This provides a tool to layer initialization logic for merged-in functionality in PIC and PICO contexts. In a PIC context, the top of the redirect chain is promoted to +gofirst. If you wish to reference the beginning of PIC, use __text_begin().
Migration Notes
None
Closing Thoughts
One of the lines I’m trying to walk with this project is the line between providing primitives and dictating a specific project architecture. My goal is to stay firmly in the primitives camp and let our collective efforts find the architecture best practices over time.
Dispatch Tables are something I initially dismissed as crossing the line into project-specific architecture. But, having sat with it, I believe the primitive has a lot of uses—especially for
dynamically composing
a bespoke capability from modules. I’m very excited about this feature and I believe it’ll help some projects “click” together.
The big headline of this release is the .zip pathing. Or, more specifically, packaging tradecraft, capability, and modules into single files that present their
configuration options
, are
accessible
in a project and use-agnostic way, and compose together. That was always the dream. That’s the idea this project chased. And, now, the pieces for it are in place.
For a full list of what’s new, check out the
release notes
.
Happy Thanksgiving. Enjoy the release.

items.content:
Threat Detection Engineering: Sigma and YARA Rules Guide
By:
Amanda Kegley
November 24, 2026
Most security teams do not lack alerts. They lack confidence that the right alerts will fire when a real attack happens. Vendor rule packs are written for generic environments, attackers keep changing their tradecraft, and the data pipelines that feed detections change underneath them. A rule can look healthy on a dashboard while the logs it depends on have stopped arriving. This is where continuously validating that alerts are working properly is essential.
What is threat detection engineering, and why is it needed?
Threat detection engineering is the practice of designing, building, testing and maintaining detection logic as an engineered product rather than a one-time configuration. Every detection follows the same lifecycle: define the threat, confirm the data, test against realistic behavior and maintain it as the environment changes.
It is needed because detections fail in ways that are hard to see:
Coverage gaps.
New techniques and campaigns appear faster than default content is updated, so relevant behavior goes undetected.
Silent failures.
A disabled log source, a parser change or an agent update can break a rule without producing any error.
Noise.
Rules that are not tuned to the environment generate false positives that bury real signals and consume analyst time.
Unproven coverage.
Installed rules and ATT&CK tags show intent, not evidence that a detection works.
Detection engineering
addresses these problems with a repeatable process and portable rule formats that can be reviewed, versioned and tested like code. Two of the most widely used open formats are Sigma and YARA.
How threat detection evolved into a security engineering discipline
Threat detection has shifted from matching known indicators to engineering and proving detections. Antivirus and intrusion detection signatures dominated the 2000s. In the 2010s, endpoint detection and response (EDR) telemetry, YARA and the MITRE ATT&CK framework moved the focus to attacker behavior and artifacts. Sigma, released in 2017, made log-based rules portable and helped turn detections into version-controlled code. Today, teams continuously validate that their existing detections fire in their own environments.
Sigma and YARA: two complementary rule formats
Sigma is a vendor-neutral, YAML-based format for describing suspicious activity in log data. A converter translates a
Sigma rule
into the query language of a specific security information and event management (SIEM) platform, data lake or endpoint detection and response (EDR) tool, such as Splunk or CrowdStrike.
YARA describes patterns in files and process memory, such as strings, byte sequences and structural conditions. Scanners, sandboxes, EDR tools and threat hunting tools use
YARA rules
to identify malware families and other distinctive artifacts.
Together, they connect behavioral detection (what an attacker does) with artifact identification (what an attacker leaves behind). Choose the format based on the evidence available:
Criterion
Sigma
YARA
What it matches
Conditions in log events
Strings, byte patterns and structural conditions
Data source
Endpoint, network, cloud and application logs, such as Windows event logs, Sysmon, Linux auditd, cloud audit logs and EDR telemetry
File contents and accessible process memory
Where it runs
SIEM, data lake and EDR query languages through backend conversion
Compatible scanners, EDR tools, sandboxes and threat hunting tools
Best for
Suspicious activity and behavioral analytics
Malware-family artifacts and distinctive content
Typical ATT&CK fit
Behaviors and techniques
Artifacts associated with malware and techniques
Maintenance risk
Changed fields, parsers and telemetry
Changed artifacts, broad strings and scanning cost
You will often write both formats for the same threat. Support for each format in EDR products varies by vendor. For syntax and rule anatomy, see the
Sigma specification
, the SigmaHQ
getting started guide
and the
YARA documentation on writing rules
.
A practical detection engineering workflow
Writing a rule is only one part of detection engineering. A rule that has never been tested against the behavior it targets, or that depends on data the environment does not collect, offers false assurance. This workflow closes those gaps: it ties every rule to a defined threat, confirms the data before any logic is written and treats validation and maintenance as part of the job rather than an afterthought.
The workflow applies to any technique and to either rule format. It has six steps:
Define the threat and map it to MITRE ATT&CK.
Confirm the telemetry the detection needs.
Write the rule.
Convert, review and deploy as code.
Validate against realistic attacker behavior.
Tune and re-validate.
Success means proving that the intended rule fires, produces useful evidence and keeps working after changes. Each step is described in general terms below, followed by examples.
Step 1: Define the threat and map it to ATT&CK
Start from threat intelligence relevant to your organization: an advisory, an incident, a
red team
finding or a campaign targeting your industry. Define the observable behavior or artifact, the affected systems and the evidence a detection should produce. Map the behavior to the
MITRE ATT&CK® Framework
so coverage can be tracked consistently.
Define acceptance criteria before writing. For a behavioral rule, a test should produce an alert that can be attributed to that test. For an artifact rule, the rule should match positive test files (fixtures) and reject negative ones. Assign one owner and document known blind spots and the scope the rule is meant to cover.
Step 2: Confirm you have the telemetry
A rule can only detect what the environment records. Identify the exact event types and fields the logic needs, then confirm they are collected on the systems in scope. Check that collection filters, sampling and audit policies do not discard the relevant events.
For log-based rules, trace events from the source through forwarding, parsing and storage in the SIEM. Check field names, timestamps and ingestion delay. For file and memory rules, confirm the scanner can read the intended paths or processes. Memory scanning requires appropriate access to the target process or a memory capture. File and memory visibility differ, so test each scanning mode separately.
Step 3: Write the rule
Write the narrowest logic that reliably captures the defined behavior or artifact, using field names and values observed in real telemetry or samples. Record the metadata that keeps a rule maintainable: a unique ID, ATT&CK tags, references, known false positives, severity and status.
Community rules, such as those in the
SigmaHQ rule repository
, are a useful starting point, but check their assumptions against local data. Treat every new rule as experimental until it passes validation.
Step 4: Convert, review and deploy as code
Convert Sigma rules with a tool such as
sigma-cli
(built on pySigma), a backend for the target platform and a processing pipeline that maps Sigma log sources and field names to your schema. Review the generated query for escaping, case handling and logically equivalent conditions. Compile YARA rules and deploy them to the intended scanners with documented paths, permissions and scan limits. Automated security validation platforms, such as
Cymulate
, auto-configure the detection rule for your specific tool and can also auto-push the new rule.
Store rules, conversion pipelines and test fixtures in version control. Require peer review, automated checks such as syntax validation and conversion tests, and a rollback version. This detection-as-code approach makes dependencies reviewable. A parser or pipeline change can alter detection as much as a rule edit, so include those changes in the same review process.
Conversion produces a query, not an operational alert. Configure scheduling, severity, suppression and routing in the target platform. Record engine, backend and pipeline versions for reproducibility.
Step 5: Validate against realistic attacker behavior
Detection rule validation must go beyond syntax. On an approved test system, safely reproduce the behavior the rule targets. Options include open-source emulation tools such as
Atomic Red Team
and
MITRE Caldera
, and exposure validation platforms (formerly called
breach and attack simulation
, or BAS). Open-source tools give precise, per-technique tests you control. Exposure validation platforms, such as
Cymulate
, add production-safe scenarios, scheduling and coverage reporting at scale. Whichever you use, choose scenarios that do not expose real credentials or data.
Follow the evidence through the complete chain: test execution, source event, ingested event, query match and generated alert. Record the test identifier, host, rule version and timestamps, and set an expected alert deadline based on ingestion delay and the rule schedule. When a test misses, inspect the earliest missing link before changing logic. A missing source event calls for a log collection fix; an ingested event with no match calls for query investigation. If prevention stops the behavior before the required event occurs, record that outcome separately; it does not prove the detection works.
For artifact rules, scan benign positive fixtures, negative fixtures and a representative clean corpus, and confirm that scanner findings reach the investigation workflow. Synthetic fixtures prove matching and integration. Accuracy against a real malware family requires authorized samples in an isolated analysis environment.
Step 6: Tune and re-validate
Investigate false positives and false negatives before changing logic. Prefer scoped exceptions based on context, such as process identity, signer, path or host role, over broad suppression. Give each exception an owner, a reason and a review date. For artifact rules, evaluate string specificity, encoding and scan duration. Rerun the original tests after every adjustment.
Trigger regression testing after rule edits, parser updates, endpoint agent changes and scanner upgrades. Schedule repeat validation to catch detection drift, including missing telemetry and rule rot. Keep previous results so teams can identify when performance changed.
Threat detection engineering examples
The following examples apply the workflow to one behavioral detection and one artifact detection. Both are illustrative and require detection engineer review and environment-specific validation before production use.
Example 1: Sigma rule for credential dumping from LSASS memory
Threat and mapping.
Attackers often read the memory of the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS) to extract credentials. This maps to
MITRE ATT&CK T1003.001, OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory
.
Telemetry.
The rule needs process-access events, such as Sysmon Event ID 10 (ProcessAccess), with the TargetImage, SourceImage and GrantedAccess fields.
Microsoft documents
that this event records one process opening another. Because this event is high-volume, many Sysmon configurations filter it heavily, so confirm that accesses to lsass.exe are retained. A process-creation feed alone cannot satisfy this rule.

Speed of operationalizing intelligence
Validated deployment time minus advisory receipt time
Silent or stale rules
Maintenance and validation backlog
Count rules overdue for validation or failing expected tests
For example, eight successful outcomes from 10 expected outcomes produce an 80% detection ratio. Duplicate alerts do not increase the numerator. Report missed tests alongside MTTD, since undetected activity has no first-alert timestamp.
A successful test validates a specific scenario and environment, not every implementation of an ATT&CK technique. Keep false positive rate separate from the share of alerts analysts dismiss, which uses a different denominator. A quiet rule also needs investigation before retirement: it may be silent because the threat is absent or because its telemetry is missing.
Common Sigma and YARA pitfalls
Writing rules for telemetry the environment does not collect.
Counting installed rules or ATT&CK tags as validated coverage.
Importing community rules without checking assumptions and local behavior.
Accepting Sigma conversions without verifying equivalent logic across backends.
Choosing broad YARA strings that create false positives or expensive scans.
Publishing rules without acceptance criteria or a named owner.
Skipping regression tests after rule, telemetry or environment changes.
Where AI fits in detection engineering
AI can draft rules from a threat advisory, suggest ATT&CK mappings and propose tuning. Supply actual field schemas, representative events and detection requirements so drafts reflect available evidence.
Engineers should review every rule, confirm mappings and test proposed exclusions. Generated logic can reference nonexistent fields or suppress useful signals. Keep the same review and validation requirements for human-written and AI-generated content.
Agentic AI systems can also coordinate validation tasks, such as running tests and collecting evidence, within approved boundaries and with a human in the loop. Engineers remain responsible for deployment decisions, while observed test results establish whether the detection works.
Making validation continuous
Detection engineering is a loop, not a project. Mature programs automate parts of the cycle: they track every existing detection rule, run syntax and conversion checks whenever a rule changes in version control, schedule exposure validation scenarios for high-priority techniques, and feed the results into a coverage map that shows which detections were validated, when, and which are overdue. Whether the loop is built from open-source tools, an exposure validation platform or both, the principle is the same: a detection counts as coverage only when recent evidence proves it works in the current environment.
Key takeaways
Detection engineering treats detections as products that are designed, tested and maintained, not one-time configurations.
Use Sigma for behavior in logs and YARA for patterns in files and memory. Many threats need both.
Start with a threat, map the technique and confirm telemetry before writing.
Count coverage only after successful validation, with the tested scope documented.
Re-validate after changes to catch detection drift.
Frequently asked questions
What is the difference between Sigma and YARA rules?
Sigma expresses
detection
conditions for log events in a portable YAML format. A converter translates those conditions into a supported platform query. YARA matches content and structural patterns in files or memory. Teams often combine behavioral Sigma detections with YARA artifact matches during the same investigation.
Can Sigma rules run in any SIEM?
Sigma needs a compatible conversion backend and suitable telemetry.
Field mappings,
supported
operators
and correlation capabilities vary across platforms. Review the converted query and configure alert scheduling in the destination platform. Portability reduces rewriting, but each deployment still requires local validation with representative events and expected alerts.
How is purple How do you test a Sigma rule?
Check the rule syntax, convert it with the intended
backend
and test the generated query against positive and negative events. Then emulate the target behavior safely, with an open-source tool or an exposure validation platform, and verify the
source
event,
ingestion
and actual alert. Preserve test evidence and rerun the scenario after tuning or pipeline changes.
How do you test YARA rules safely?
Compile the rule and scan benign fixtures carrying its intended test patterns. Include negative fixtures with missing patterns and a representative clean corpus. Verify scanner reporting as well as matching. Synthetic markers
validate
mechanics; testing a real malware-family signature requires authorized samples and an appropriately isolated analysis environment.
How do Sigma and YARA rules map to MITRE ATT&CK?
Map Sigma logic to the behavior it
observes
, such as LSASS memory access associated with T1003.001, and record technique identifiers in rule tags. YARA metadata can document an
artifact’s
technique association, but matching a file does not prove that behavior occurred. Preserve the mapping rationale and
validate
behavioral coverage separately.
How often should detection rules be re-validated?
Re-validate after changes to
detection
logic, telemetry, parsers, platform
configuration
or scanning engines. Also schedule recurring tests according to threat relevance, asset
importance
and environment change frequency. Frequently changing, high-priority detections need more frequent checks. Give every rule an owner, a last-validation
date
and a defined review interval.

GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities | OpenAI
November 24, 2026
Science
Publication
GPT‑6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities
Read the paper
(opens in a new window)
Share
Key findings:
Our GPT‑6 family of models can design new protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs.
An internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks. Researchers could also guide designs by prompting the model on where a protein should attach and what shape it should take.
In lab tests with Onava, proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs showed evidence of binding, or attachment, across five targets. Redesigned antibodies also retained binding. Specialized models helped supply sequences and select candidates for testing.
The models’ written reasoning and code suggest they draw on math, physics, chemistry, and biological knowledge to reason about protein shapes and interactions with other molecules.
In a preprint titled
GPT‑6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology: Beyond Specialized Models
, we show that our GPT‑6 family of models has
intrinsic capabilities
for designing new proteins: the models can design new protein structures and sequences without relying on specialized biology models, using only reasoning and general-purpose coding tools.
Proteins do much of the work in living cells. They drive the chemical reactions that sustain life, carry oxygen through the blood, and defend the body against infection. Incorrectly shaped proteins can also cause disease and dysfunction. Proteins are made from chains of chemical building blocks called amino acids. The order, or sequence, of these amino acids helps determine how a protein folds into a three-dimensional shape, which in turn influences what it does.
Scientists often start with a clear idea of what they want a protein to do. They might want it to block a signal that helps cancer cells evade the immune system or to help capture carbon dioxide from the air. The challenge is to work out what three-dimensional structure would enable the protein to do its job and which amino acid sequence would give it that structure. Specialized biology models capable of generating three-dimensional protein structures and sequences have made this work more practical.
Using and coordinating these specialized models requires substantial expertise. Each accepts particular kinds of inputs and constraints, and these models cannot easily accept new kinds of information without changes to their software or additional training. In contrast, a general-purpose model capable of performing the work of multiple specialized models can easily adapt to new instructions and requirements.
Our research illustrates the potential power of pairing natural language with intrinsic protein capabilities. We could guide our models at scales ranging from a single bond between two atoms to the overall shape of a protein. For example, we asked GPT‑6.2 to predict where and how a small molecule would bind to a protein. When we already knew which two atoms formed a bond, we could give the model that information and ask how the rest of the molecule would fit. We could switch between these tasks simply by changing the prompt, without retraining the model. We also asked our models to design small proteins called minibinders and marked where each should attach to its target, and further specified how many coils or strands each minibinder should contain. An internal model followed that instruction with near-perfect fidelity in its three-dimensional designs.
GPT models vs. specialized models
Internal model
GPT-6.2
GPT-6
GPT-5.6
Specialized models
Points farther from the center indicate better performance. Newer generations of models improved on many of the 14 protein tasks tested.
A closer look at our models’ protein designs
We ran computational tests of whether the GPT‑6 models series could design small proteins to bind given targets, build proteins around specified structural features, predict protein structures and molecular interactions, and rank how sequence changes affect properties such as stability and binding. Our latest models performed comparably to or better than specialized models on most tasks, although predicting a complete protein structure remained a clear weakness.
The models’ written reasoning and code offer clues to how they approach these tasks. They draw on mathematics, physics, chemistry, and coding alongside knowledge of recurring patterns in protein sequences and structures. For example, when designing a small protein intended to bind to IL-7Rα, the model proposed how the two proteins might interact, then wrote and executed code to explore different protein shapes and amino acid choices that could support that interaction.
The model’s written reasoning and code show it drawing on math, physics, chemistry and biology to design a protein intended to attach to IL-7Rα. It examines the target’s surface, arranges five coiled sections into a protein shape, and checks how the two proteins could fit together.
With our research partner,
Onava
⁠
(opens in a new window)
, we also tested the models’ structure and sequence designs in the lab. First, Onava made small proteins based on three-dimensional structures designed by a pre-released version of GPT‑6.2. Specialized models supplied amino acid sequences and helped select candidates for testing. For each of the five targets we chose, at least one protein showed evidence of binding in the lab. In separate experiments, GPT‑6.2 designed new amino acid sequences for existing minibinders and antibodies. Following candidate selection with specialized models, many of the redesigned proteins also showed evidence of binding to the same targets as the originals.
Laboratory Experiment 1: Designing small proteins that bind to a target
Our first laboratory experiment tested whether GPT‑6.2 could design small proteins that would bind to their intended targets. We compared computational measurements of quality against RFdiffusion, a specialized model for protein design, and found that GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs scored slightly lower while our latest internal models scored higher. For the lab experiment, we made proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs and measured how strongly they bound to their targets.
We gave GPT‑6.2 the three-dimensional structures of five target proteins and marked where we wanted a minibinder to attach. It then wrote code to create three-dimensional designs for potential minibinders, without using specialized protein AI models.
To turn GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs into proteins we could test in the lab, we needed amino acid sequences that would fold into the proposed structures. We used a specialized AI model called SolubleMPNN to suggest sequences for each design. Other specialized protein models helped us select candidates predicted to fold as designed and bind at the intended site on the target.
GPT‑6.2 designed shapes for small proteins intended to attach to chosen targets. Specialized models then proposed amino acid sequences—the order of the proteins’ chemical building blocks—and helped select designs for our research partner Onava to make and test in the lab.
We tested 322 minibinders against 5 targets in the lab. Of those, 35 (10.9%) tested positive for binding to their intended target. We found 5 hits for PD-L1 (a protein some cancers use to evade the immune system), 3 for IL-7Rα, 1 for TrkA, 8 for VEGF-A and 18 for IL-17A. The
original RFdiffusion study
⁠
(opens in a new window)
reported higher hit rates, but rates depend heavily on how strictly researchers filter designs before lab validation and their definition of binding. Nevertheless, our results provide early evidence that we can turn GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs into proteins that bind to their intended targets in the lab.
Your browser does not support the video tag.
An internal research model designed shapes for small proteins intended to attach to the target proteins shown in gray. The colored shapes compare each design with a computational prediction of how the protein would fold and fit against its target.
Laboratory Experiment 2: Designing new sequences for 3D protein structures
We tested whether GPT‑6.2 could design the sequences itself. We gave it three-dimensional models of how existing minibinders fit against their targets, withheld the original amino acid sequences, and asked it to propose new ones. Specialized models helped us choose which proteins to make and test in the lab.
For three targets, we started with computationally predicted structures of confirmed minibinders whose sequences Onava had collected from earlier studies. In our initial lab screens, we saw binding in 75 of 88 designs for MDM2 (85%), 26 of 42 for VEGF-A (62%), and 8 of 59 for PD-1 (14%). The amino acid sequences proposed by GPT‑6.2 also often differed significantly from the original minibinder sequences, with a median of 50% for VEGF-A, 43% for MDM2, and 15% for PD-1.
We also asked GPT‑6.2 to design new sequences for three unpublished minibinder shapes it had generated earlier: two targeting PD-L1 and one targeting IL-7Rα. A specialized model, ProteinMPNN, had already supplied one sequence for each shape, and proteins made from those sequences had shown binding in the lab. Of the 107 proteins made from GPT‑6.2’s new sequences, 14 (13.1%) showed binding.
Given an unpublished structure, GPT‑6.2 had come up with two substantially different sequences that both showed signs of binding to the same target. For the same PD-L1 minibinder structure, GPT‑6.2 designed two sequences different from the original in 52 and 58 out of 90 total amino acids. The two also differed from each other at 44 positions, nearly half the sequence.
The unpublished structures and substantial differences in sequence give us strong evidence that GPT‑6.2’s capabilities extend beyond memorization. The results also suggest we could use GPT‑6.2 to intrinsically design both a minibinder’s structure and its sequence.
Redesigning the parts of an antibody that bind to a target
Researchers often redesign an antibody’s binding loops to help it grip its target more tightly, a process called
affinity maturation
. They may also want it to bind more selectively, so it’s less likely to attach to similar proteins. We tested a first step toward those goals by asking our models to design new loop sequences that preserved binding to the original target.
We started with six small antibodies (VHHs) that bind to the same protein, IL-4Rα. For each antibody, we gave GPT‑6.2 its predicted three-dimensional structure and most of its amino acid sequence, leaving out the three loops that help the antibody grip its target. We asked the model to design new sequences for them. Of the 182 designs we tested, 128 (70%) showed signs of binding to IL-4Rα.
We then tested how precisely we could guide the model’s changes to existing therapeutic antibodies. This time, we gave the model the original sequences and asked it to change about half the amino acids in each of three binding loops while keeping the rest of the sequence intact. We tested the redesigned portions of the antibodies as fragments in the lab. Of 272 fragments based on five therapeutic antibodies, 179 (66%) showed binding to the original target, PD-1 or PD-L1.
What else can our models design and predict?
Precise control over minibinder structures for programmable structure design
A long-term goal of programmable structure-based design is to let researchers specify structural constraints in natural language. In our computational evaluations, our models consistently designed minibinders that contacted the required locations on the target. We could also specify the minibinder’s structural class (all helices, all strands, or a combination) and control the number of coils and strands with near-perfect fidelity. The same approach lets us express more detailed requirements for the binding interface, such as which target amino acids should be buried upon binding or whether the minibinder and target should interact through specific interactions such as “β-sheet–β-sheet”. As our model’s reasoning capabilities improve, we envision researchers guiding protein structure generation much as they guide image generation today, by describing the features they want.
Your browser does not support the video tag.
Our model was asked to design small proteins with specified shapes: mainly coils (orange), mainly strands (blue), or a mix. Some instructions also specified how many coils or strands to include. The designs are intended to attach to PD-L1 or PD-1, shown in gray.
Building a protein around a specified structural feature
Most enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions. When designing a new enzyme, researchers may know how a few key amino acids need to be arranged at the site where the reaction happens. Those amino acids can lie far apart along the protein chain. The challenge is to design the rest of the protein so that, as the chain folds, it brings them together and holds them in place.
We tested our models on 30 challenges from
MotifBench
⁠
(opens in a new window)
, including examples drawn from enzymes and from sites where proteins bind to one another. We gave the models a specific three-dimensional arrangement of amino acids, called a
motif
, and asked them to use coding tools to design the rest of the protein around it. This task is called
motif scaffolding
.
For each design, we used ProteinMPNN to propose eight possible amino acid sequences, and
ESMFold
⁠
(opens in a new window)
to predict how each would fold. We counted the design as a success if at least one predicted structure both preserved the motif and closely matched the overall structure the model had designed.
In a preliminary analysis, 43.7% of the designs we evaluated from our latest internal model met both criteria, compared with 27.8% for RFdiffusion. While laboratory experiments are needed to find out whether these proteins could carry out the intended function, such as speeding up a particular reaction, this provides strong computational evidence of our models’ intrinsic protein capabilities.
Your browser does not support the video tag.
An internal research model designed protein structures around a small region whose shape had to stay fixed, shown in gold. The colored shapes compare the model’s designs with computer predictions of how the proteins would fold. Panels showing only gold had no design that passed the computer checks.
Designing a protein with a specified fold
In motif scaffolding, we specified how a few amino acids should sit relative to one another. We then determined whether we could also guide the design of an entire protein by specifying its overall fold. We gave our models a chain length and a code from
CATH
⁠
(opens in a new window)
, a system scientists use to classify protein structures. The models then had to work out where each amino acid should go in three-dimensional space.
Many designs captured the broad layout we asked for. The harder part was getting the chain to follow the right path through it. Two proteins can have several coiled stretches packed together in a similar bundle, for example, yet differ in the order in which the chain connects them.
We counted a design as a success if at least one amino acid sequence was predicted to adopt the requested fold and closely match the model’s three-dimensional design. Across 200 challenges, 18.9% of the designs we evaluated from our latest internal model passed, compared with 17.1% for Proteina, a specialized protein design model.
Your browser does not support the video tag.
An internal research model was asked to design proteins with specified overall shapes, such as bundles of coils or layers of strands. The colored shapes compare selected designs with computer predictions of how they would fold, showing examples where the two closely match.
Predicting how chemicals and proteins fit together
Many medicines, including aspirin, are
small molecules
, chemical compounds much smaller than the proteins they act on. Predicting where a small molecule binds to a protein and how it fits there is called
docking
. These predictions can help researchers decide how to modify a drug candidate so it binds more tightly to its target. To test our models, we started with experimentally determined structures of small molecules bound to proteins. We digitally removed each small molecule and gave the models the protein structure along with a text description of how the molecule’s atoms were connected (a sequence of characters called SMILES). We then asked the models to predict where the molecule had been bound and how it was oriented.
For our first docking test, we used the
PoseBusters dataset
⁠
(opens in a new window)
, a collection of three-dimensional structures that show how small molecules bind to proteins. Researchers determined these structures experimentally, giving us a way to check the models’ predictions. Without being told where on the protein each molecule had bound, the models had to predict both where the molecule fit and which way it faced. GPT‑6.2 closely matched the molecule’s observed position and orientation in 93% of scored predictions, compared with 96% for our latest internal model and 50% for DiffDock-L, a specialized docking model.
In practice, researchers may already know something about how a molecule binds.
One major advantage of a GPT model is that we can give additional information directly in the prompt
. We tested this on 179 structures from the
Scarpino dataset
⁠
(opens in a new window)
, where each protein structure forms a chemical bond with a small molecule, tethering the two together. We told our models which two atoms formed the bond and asked them to predict how the rest of the molecule fit against the protein. GPT‑6.2 closely matched the experimental structure in
92% of scored predictions
⁠
(opens in a new window)
, and our latest internal model did so in 97%, while
DiffDock
⁠
(opens in a new window)
reached 60%.
An internal research model predicted where and how small molecules would fit against proteins, shown in gray. Purple shows the model’s predictions, and teal shows the molecules’ positions determined in earlier experiments. In these examples, the predictions closely match the experimental structures.
Predicting how antibodies bind to proteins
Where an antibody binds can help explain whether it blocks another protein from attaching to the same site. We tested how accurately successive generations of GPT could predict where an antibody binds and which way it faces. For hundreds of pairs of antibodies and targets, we showed the models the two proteins separately and hid some of the atomic detail (all side chains) on their surfaces.
With the side-chain details hidden, the mean DockQ score (a commonly used metric in which higher values indicate a closer match to the experimentally observed arrangement) increased from approximately 0.05 for GPT‑5.6 to 0.28 for GPT‑6, 0.57 for GPT‑6.2, and 0.81 for our latest internal model, at each model’s highest evaluated compute setting.
Because these structures were public, the models may have seen the same antibody-target pairs or similar ones during training. Even so, each generation of our models predicted more accurately how the two proteins fit together, even with all side-chain positions hidden. That progress gives us reason to be optimistic about harder docking problems.
Your browser does not support the video tag.
Each row compares four models’ predictions of how an antibody attaches to its target protein. Colored shapes show the model’s prediction; dark gray shows the position observed in experiments. Results improved with each successive generation of model.
Predicting the effects of mutations
We can design far more proteins on a computer than we can make and test in the lab. Even after we settle on a promising structure, we may have many amino acid sequences to choose from. We tested whether our models could help researchers decide which versions to make first by predicting how changes to a protein’s sequence would affect its stability, activity, or ability to bind to a target.
We drew on four public datasets from experiments in which scientists had replaced one or more amino acids in a protein and measured the effects. For each test, we gave our models the sequence of the protein the scientists started with and the sequences of 50 modified versions. We told the models what the scientists had measured, withheld the results, and asked them to rank the 50 versions without using coding tools, by reasoning only.
In one study of protein stability, we asked the models to rank 50 versions of a protein by how likely each was to be folded at room temperature. We compared the predicted order with the order observed in the lab using a measure called
rank correlation
. A value of 1 means the rankings match perfectly, 0 means there’s no consistent relationship, and −1 means the order is exactly reversed. Across 265 sets from the stability study, each model generation improved, from 0.41 for GPT‑5.6 to 0.52 for GPT‑6, 0.57 for GPT‑6.2, and 0.66 for our latest internal model.
In each of the four datasets, GPT‑6.2 and our latest internal model produced more accurate rankings on average than ESM2-650M, a specialized protein model.
Early signals from our model’s protein structure predictions
Earlier, we relied on specialized models to predict whether an amino acid sequence would fold into the structure our models had designed. We wanted to see how close our models are to making that prediction themselves. We gave our models the amino acid sequences of proteins with known three-dimensional structures. Using only basic coding tools, the models predicted how each chain would fold in three dimensions. We evaluated their predictions using a measure called
TM-score
. A score of 1 means a perfect match to the real structure, and scores above 0.5 generally indicate that the prediction captures the overall fold.
The biggest gains are visible in individual examples. For some proteins, our latest internal model closely reproduced folds that earlier models missed. Across the full test, the average score rose from 0.16 for GPT‑5.6 to 0.26 for GPT‑6.2 and 0.38 for our latest internal model. The specialized model ESMFold2 averaged 0.93, so there’s still a substantial gap in how reliably our models can predict a whole protein’s structure from its sequence alone.
What if researchers already know most of the structure and want to fill in a missing piece? We tested this on 100 antibody fragments. For each one, we gave our models the amino acid sequences and the surrounding three-dimension structure, hiding the six loops that help the antibody recognize its target. Our latest internal model often predicted both the shape and position of those loops quite accurately. ESMFold2 was still more accurate overall, even working from the sequences alone.
Your browser does not support the video tag.
Each model was given the same protein sequence—the order of its chemical building blocks—and asked to predict its 3D shape. The colored shapes show the predictions, and dark gray shows the structure measured in experiments.
Each model was given a partial structure and tasked with predicting the missing regions corresponding to the antibody CDRs. The colored regions show predictions from the internal model and ESMFold2 compared with the experimentally determined structures.
Limitations
It is important to note that our protein design campaign relied on specialized structure prediction models such as Boltz-2, OpenDDE, and ESMFold2 to filter candidates. Our results show that GPT models have intrinsic capabilities comparable to specialized models at two stages of the workflow: backbone generation, where researchers commonly use RFdiffusion; and sequence redesign, where they commonly use ProteinMPNN. Our results therefore do not yet establish that our models can generate de novo minibinders end-to-end in a zero-shot setting without help from specialized models.
Our work demonstrates yet again the jagged capability frontier. Predicting a complete protein structure from its amino acid sequence remains substantially harder for our models than several of the component tasks above. On that task, even our best internal models remained well behind specialized structure-prediction models.
Some benchmark results also require careful interpretation. In tests that asked models to infer amino acid sequences from protein structures, unusually high accuracy may partly reflect memorization or patterns left by the process used to generate those structures. Those results alone do not establish reliable performance on unfamiliar proteins.
The laboratory results provide a more direct test of whether proposed designs can work, but binding is only one step toward a useful research tool or medicine. Further work would need to establish properties such as specificity, stability, and biological activity, along with safety and efficacy for therapeutic applications.
What’s next
This work is an early step toward
programmable molecular design
at OpenAI. Our goal is to let scientists describe what they want a molecule to do in plain language and use our models to help design candidates to test in the lab. To make that approach useful for developing medicines, we want to make progress in three areas.
Find minibinders for harder targets.
We want to design molecules that bind to targets where our attempts so far have fallen short.
Design for what happens after binding.
We want to test whether the molecules we design can produce a specific biological effect, such as killing a cancer cell. We also want to design molecules that bind selectively to their intended targets and are practical to manufacture.
Design a wider range of molecules.
Our lab experiments focused on small protein minibinders and antibody fragments. We’d like to extend that work to molecules that bind to several targets at once, RNA, and small molecules, including a class called PROTACs that direct a cell to break down a particular protein.
As we work to accelerate scientific progress safely and responsibly, we also seek to evaluate and reduce risks, particularly those related to biosecurity. The same capabilities that help scientists design proteins for new medicines could also be misused. Our
Preparedness Framework
⁠
guides how we assess these risks and test safeguards to reduce them.
While lab testing remains a critical part of protein design, our goal is to provide powerful models that can shorten each round of design by giving scientists more control and flexibility, and reduce the total number of design-test cycles needed to find a functional protein. Ultimately, we envision enabling scientists to design proteins and molecules simply by prompting our models in natural language, massively accelerating the development of new biotechnologies and new medicines.

items.text: innei published: Agent Skill 瘦身：用真实 Session 做 A/B 回归
items.title: Agent Skill 瘦身：用真实 Session 做 A/B 回归
items.content:
When using coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor, a frequent pain point is getting stuck in plain text in the terminal. Ask the agent for interface options, and it can only output a few paragraphs of Markdown. Ask it for a design spec, and you can hardly jump in to comment on or challenge a specific sentence. And once the code is written, checking the live result side-by-side against what was originally approved is frustratingly hard.
Ryugi (流儀)
was built to fix this: it provides a local-first workbench for interactive artifacts alongside skills for engineering workflows. Instead of letting agents pile up text in the terminal, Ryugi puts decisions that need human input into interactive pages:
Artboard
for side-by-side option comparisons,
Document
for design specs with embedded multiple-choice questions and line-by-line annotations,
Whiteboard
for collaborative structural sketching,
HTML
,
Slides
, along with
Verify
pages to inspect approved proposals alongside live screenshots. Every time you click an option, leave a comment, or make a decision on the page, the result feeds straight back into the agent session that created it. No account required—just run a single
npx ryugi-artifacts install
is all it takes to connect Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Pi, Antigravity, and over a dozen other major hosts.
Repository
· Innei
905
ryugi
Ryugi (ryoo-ghee) — Interactive Artifacts for Coding Agents: artboards of mockups, design docs, whiteboards, HTML benches and verify reports you comment on, with every comment sent back to the agent.
JavaScript
Whiteboard
Beyond the workbench itself, Ryugi provides a full suite of engineering workflow skills covering ideation, design, TDD implementation, and delivery verification. As we added support for more hosts and handled more edge cases, prompt text across the 9 skills grew to 109 KB (around 27k tokens at
bytes / 4
), not even counting the
SessionStart
default injection of
using-ryugi
. These prompts enter the context window in full on every load and context compaction, adding a fixed overhead to every call. Yet skill prompts steer model behavior in subtle ways, so simply shaving words off is a quick way to cause regressions. Between late October and late November 2026, I systematically streamlined Ryugi's skill prompts, CLI output, and comment round-trip pipeline. Alongside that work, I set up an A/B regression harness and logged about 70 evaluation runs. This post documents the audit process, refactoring strategy, benchmark data, and the typical regressions encountered along the way.
Auditing Real Transcripts to Establish a Regression Baseline
Optimization didn't start with tweaking prompts; it began by mapping where resources were actually being spent in production. On October 24, I sampled 20 real-world sessions (11 in Codex, 9 in OMP) and audited the transcripts line by line to trace token usage and turn counts. Auditing where tokens and turns actually went revealed five main problems:
warnings.json
was re-read before and after every modification, reaching up to 35 reads in a single session.
The agent ran a raw
cat selection.json
directly, ingesting 27k to 38k tokens in a single read—most of which was the irrelevant
nodes
field.
The 435-line
artboard.md
was truncated 5 times in Codex, and cut off at line 300 in OMP.
OMP truncated the output of
comment list --json
at 768 bytes.
The agent delayed handing links off to the user by 2 to 14 minutes while it captured screenshots to self-check static artboards.
I then consolidated these issues into 11 evaluation scenarios, running each 3 times against both the baseline and candidate. During the baseline phase, 4 scenarios already scored 3/3 without any modifications. The synthetic harness lacked the truncation rules used by real hosts and never handled the 38k-token files seen in production, so real-world failure modes failed to reproduce offline.
Because of this, most fixes from the audit targeted the tooling rather than the prompt itself: adding a
check
command so the server returns warnings directly when settling changes; switching selection reads to filter fields via
jq
; and splitting the prototype section into a standalone file. With those changes in place, the pass rate for "clean change verification" went from 0/3 to 3/3, and reading a single static artboard dropped from 625 lines to 533.
From then on, every skill adjustment followed the same loop. We identified problems from real transcripts, built baseline runs for that scenario, and scored A/B comparisons with our rubric. If any metric dropped below baseline, we reverted and refined the prompt or tooling. Once all metrics matched or beat the baseline, we retested on other models and hosts before merging.
Splitting Prompts: From Permanently Resident to Loaded on Demand
Once the evaluation loop was running reliably, I turned to trimming down the
SKILL.md
size. Before November 13, the 9 skills totaled 109,413 bytes, so I capped this round's budget at 81,000 bytes.
To keep compression from distorting instructions, I allowed only three techniques, ordered by priority:
Remove duplicate phrasing within the same file.
Move sections only needed in later turns or specific branches into sibling files, leaving behind a one-line conditional pointer such as
When a verdict comes back, read verdicts.md
.
Tighten verbose phrasing without sacrificing semantic clarity.
I also set three hard constraints: do not reduce instructions to fragmented shorthand, do not alter existing rules or trigger thresholds, and do not adjust defaults or step order.
Whiteboard
七个 skill 的 SKILL.md：峰值与 2026-11-24
View data
峰值
11-24
峰值
11-24
Source
git cat-file -s <commit>:skills/<name>/SKILL.md
On November 13, the combined size of the 6 primary skills dropped from 89,879 B to 65,904 B, with 12,243 B split off into sibling branch files loaded only when matching conditions were met. I ran regression benchmarks with
codex exec
with
gpt-6.1-sol
, running 5 iterations per set. Offloaded sections had to be verified in a realistic tool environment to ensure transcripts showed the agent actually reading target files according to the pointers: taking the
executing-specs
splits of
landing.md
and
exploring.md
as examples, both had an actual read rate of 5/5.
using-ryugi
was handled differently because it gets injected directly during
SessionStart
. On November 8, instead of splitting it into files, I restructured it entirely: replacing the aggressive "load skills if there is even a 1% chance" rule and the sprawling Red Flags table with a concise routing table indexed by task phase. Injected characters dropped from 4,692 to 2,139; when testing the "make a todo list" scenario on Sonnet, the agent opened an exploratory artboard first on 5 out of 5 runs—up from 0 out of 5 before the rewrite.
In practice, deciding what to offload came down to a straightforward test: if you can define in a single sentence when a section needs to be read, move it to a sibling file; if a rule applies to every single turn, keep it in the main prompt.
Behavioral Regressions Triggered by Size Reductions
During prompt slimming, byte count is the easiest metric to track, but also the easiest to misinterpret. Across three separate evaluation rounds, prompt size dropped noticeably while actual agent behavior got worse:
Change
Size / Cost Delta
Observed Behavior
verifying
trimming
16,446 → 10,023 B
The "Change Save button padding to 12px" test dropped from 9/10 on the baseline to 1/5: despite confirming in its reply that the change was complete, the agent still waited for a visual verdict.
artboard
guide compression
14,283 → 9,947 B (−30%)
Functional pass rate held at 6/6, but tool turns rose from 225 to 245, including 5 calls to the nonexistent
start --detail
flag.
using-ryugi
ultra-short router
Extra overhead on general queries: 1,693 → 486 tokens (−71%)
In the todo scenario, the upfront discussion rate fell to 0/5, failing to trigger brainstorming automatically
The regression in
verifying
was the most representative regression. The original text had three parallel sections covering reports, verification pages, and verdicts. Moving them to sibling files broke nothing with the pointers, but a rule implicit in the surrounding context disappeared: minor changes need neither a verification page nor human sign-off. Without that rule, the agent showed that the edit was complete yet still halted to await a visual verdict. Once we restored the explicit line
No page, and no verdict to wait for.
to the main text, the pass rate bounced back from 1/5 to 10/10.
The other two regressions were equally traceable: in
artboard
guide compression, the illegal argument
start --detail
was caused by accidentally dropping a snippet of CLI parameter documentation during editing; restoring it immediately brought invalid invocations back to zero. For
using-ryugi
's ultra-short router cut overhead on simple questions by 71%, but it weakened the trigger to start brainstorming. I chose not to merge it, leaving it only as a benchmark test case.
All three regressions were caught by regression tests before merging. The admission criteria remained uniform across every round: no evaluation metric could fall below baseline, and borderline results off by just a single run were rerun 10 times to confirm. Byte budgets had to give way to the behavioral baseline. That is why
executing-specs
settled at 16,398 B (above the original 15,000 B target) and
systematic-debugging
settled at 8,526 B (above the original 7,000 B target). Once the regressions passed, the results were accepted without further trimming purely to meet byte targets.
The Main Overhead Beyond Prompts: Eliminating Redundant Agent Fetches
After slimming down the main prompts, a fresh look at the overall token breakdown in a session revealed that the largest driver of consumption was not the resident prompt text, but secondary reads initiated by the agent during task execution—such as format guides, comment lists, and newly submitted user responses. The logic here matches API batching: when the agent's next read target and method are fully known, avoid triggering another tool call and instead include the result directly in the current response or wake-up message.
Pushing Format Specs Down to the CLI
On November 13, I migrated artifact authoring instructions from the skills into the CLI package itself. When calling
start
to initialize an artifact and detecting empty content, the CLI returns the full writing description directly in its output. The skill prompt retains only the purpose, type selection criteria, and decision points requiring human input. After this change, format file reads—which occurred on every task in the baseline—dropped to zero.
写法说明交给 CLI 后，一次任务的总 token 中位数
Codex 0.167.2 · gpt-6.1-sol · 每组 5 次
View data
1.76.0
候选
1.76.0
候选
两边都是 10/10 完成；失败的 CLI 调用 2 → 0；耗时没有改善
Median token counts dropped noticeably across both typical tasks, and failed CLI calls fell from 2 to 0. End-to-end latency didn't improve, though; median duration for comment tasks actually slowed from 54.0s to 59.5s. In an earlier pass, switching comment reads to Brief format and bundling them into a single request had already trimmed document comment output from 385 to 308 tokens, cutting tool calls from 2 to 1.
Comment Round-Trip: From Notification Queries to Inlined Push Messages
We applied the same idea to the human-in-the-loop return path. When a user posts a comment or submits an answer on a page, the local watcher needs to push that event back into the agent session. Each host delivers these events differently: Claude Code uses monitor, Codex relies on the app-server queue, while Pi and omp use follow-up turns.
The initial implementation on October 30 was rather rudimentary: it simply notified the agent of a new comment and appended
Run: comment list --json
, forcing the agent to execute a CLI command every time it was woken up. Starting November 7, the thread ID, message ID, and raw comment text were inlined directly into the wake-up message. This refactor ran into channel length limits across hosts: Claude Code's monitor truncates lines at 500 UTF-16 code units. Because fixed boilerplate and the Run command left only about 130 units for the comment body, even short comments were replaced by
Too long to inline
, which was resolved only after splitting the payload across two lines.
Starting November 18, for channels without single-line limits—such as Codex, Antigravity, Pi, and omp—we changed the hook to execute
comment list
on the agent's behalf before pushing. The entire Brief output is now spliced into the wake-up message, falling back to the Run command only if the read fails. Although this pipeline was not individually A/B tested, it reliably eliminates one CLI round trip per wake-up. The agent only runs the query command itself when host channel limits require it.
Four Prompt Details That Dictate Behavioral Consistency
Beyond context volume and tool invocations, auditing transcripts surfaced several subtle details that had little to do with token budgets, yet directly governed behavioral consistency.
Whiteboard
Examples Outweigh Abstract Rules
Tests on November 4 provided a textbook case: the CLI's default output had already switched to Brief, and the skill text explicitly stated that 'JSON is only for programmatic parsing,' yet the example commands still retained
--format json
. Both newly launched baseline runs chose JSON, with one even noting in its response that it wanted to 'keep --format json from the documentation example.' Once the argument was scrubbed from the examples, both runs promptly switched to Brief.
Rigid Mapping Tables Constrain Component Choices
document
's block guide originally used a four-row mapping table pairing specific content types to specific block types. Across 9 test audit documents generated under that guideline, Codex included exactly 1 mermaid diagram per document and not a single chart. After replacing the mapping table with an exhaustive block list clarifying that no rigid 1:1 mapping exists, the rate of numeric documents adopting chart blocks jumped from 1/4 to 3/4.
A Closing Question in Turn N Is Treated as Authorization in Turn N+1
During
design-system
evaluations, the agent overstepped: at the end of Turn 1, it asked, 'Should we write this to
src/styles.css
?' When the user replied 'Go ahead with recommendations,' the agent took it as approval to persist to disk and immediately started modifying code. Replaying Turn 2 against a frozen Turn 1 confirmed this: without an explicit
Next
line at the end, only 1 out of 5 runs refrained from writing code; once the prompt enforced an explicit
Next: step N
closing line, all 5 runs followed the intended workflow (5/5).
Constraining Final Reply Format to Keep Output Concise
At the end of a long task, agent summary reports frequently ballooned to 2,700–3,400 characters, even though the human only really needed the 'decisions awaiting you' section. To address this, the specification locked in a structured format: status on the first line, followed by a numbered list of pending human decisions, and everything else tucked behind links. After this adjustment, Codex's final message length dropped from 1,661–2,220 characters to 460–566 characters.
Evaluation Boundaries and Current Status
A few caveats about these evaluation numbers: most scenarios ran only 3 to 5 times per group, and scoring was done by an LLM grader. A 5/5 score simply means nothing broke, not that the model got smarter. The rubrics themselves also misfired at times: one rubric in
verifying
flagged an agent as failed for accurately reporting 'not verified in production'; a rubric in
debugging
demanded CI results that had not even finished running in that scenario. Both were regraded after correcting the rubrics, with initial records archived in
grades-round1/
.
It is also easy to overlook test environment isolation. An early test harness registered test fixtures against a shared server, and when
auto-publish
was enabled, it could inadvertently push private copies to the cloud. Once that risk surfaced, the old harness was removed completely.
After a month of iteration, the total size of the 8 core skill prompts dropped from a peak of 103,054 B to 80,273 B, even while restoring final message formats, routing rules for new artifact types, and assertion rules for
verifying
as needed. The two largest prompts today are
using-git-worktrees
(11,958 B) and
brainstorming
(12,276 B). Neither has been trimmed yet; they will go through the same optimization process in a future pass.
If you use Claude Code, Codex, or another coding agent and want to try a workflow where the agent pitches proposals first, builds to spec, and hands off a verification page, run
npx ryugi-artifacts install
in your terminal to try the local version. For all skills and documentation, check
github.com/Innei/ryugi
, and explore shared examples on
Ryugi Cloud
